extracted.intended_audience: general 19th-century readers and contemporaries interested in the Maria Monk controversy / critics of the Roman Catholic clergy
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century pamphlet/chapter defending Maria Monk's 'Awful Disclosures' by recounting reception, publishing rebuttals (affidavits), and proposing tests and procedural remedies to verify or refute her allegations about convent abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical inspection of the convent ('the sight and the touch')
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct search of the premises is proposed as the decisive test of Maria Monk's allegations: 'the sight and the touch!' — a Committee of the New York Protestant Association are willing to accompany her to Montreal to walk through the Hotel Dieu Nunnery and investigate the truth without favour or partiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'that unerring criterion' which does not depend on witness credibility, conflicting evidence, personal friendship, or religious prejudices. The author offers this as the short, easy, and sensible test that would remove all possibility of deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiation of civil or criminal proceedings by the accused (test by legal action)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the priests named were truly guilty, they should vindicate themselves by coming forward and instituting civil or criminal actions against the publishers or Maria Monk; failure to do so is presented as suspicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet argues that had Lartigue, Bonin, Dufresne, Richards, etc. believed the charges false and injurious they could 'put her truth to the test' by commencing suits; their refusal to sue is used rhetorically to suggest either fear of exposure or tacit acknowledgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for direct charges against particular individuals for magistrate action
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates (Dr. Robertson's position) will take 'the necessary steps for a full investigation' only if direct charges are made against particular individuals of a criminal nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets a procedural standard for when official inquiry will proceed: unnamed/general accusations are insufficient; specific, individualized accusations are necessary to trigger warrants and formal investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborating testimony and affidavits from witnesses in the community
rubrics_metrics.description: The credibility of the story is measured by the availability of other witnesses and affidavits (e.g., Mr. Ogden, A. P. Hart, and the Montreal affidavits) who can corroborate parts of Maria Monk's account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet both cites affidavits published against Maria Monk and asserts that other witnesses in New York and Montreal are ready to appear; corroboration by local, independent persons is treated as necessary to convince skeptical magistrates and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of physical evidence of past confinement (marks, manacles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspecting the accused's body for physical signs of restraint or mistreatment (Dr. Robertson notes that 'no mark or appearance indicated the wearing of manacles') is deployed as an evidentiary point used by critics to challenge the confinement claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics use absence of visible marks to dispute claims of long confinement; the pamphlet replies by noting possible concealment methods (e.g., irons covered with soft cloths) and by emphasizing other forms of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of the accuser's character and mental state
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents challenge Maria Monk on grounds of character (immoral reputation) or occasional alienation of mind; these personal-credibility assessments are used as a criterion for dismissing or accepting her narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet records these attacks (derangement, immoral character, identity doubts) and rebuts them by offering supporting testimony (school-mates, mother) and by arguing that such charges are often levied against run-away nuns and other converts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison with independent historical accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of Maria Monk's account to prior documented exposures (e.g., Scipio de Ricci's 'Secrets of Nunneries') is advanced as supporting evidence of credibility: 'That statement is so exactly conformed to Maria Monk's "Awful Disclosures."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet treats corroboration from independent, earlier reports about convent abuses as lending weight to the new allegations, while acknowledging that resemblance could arise from similar real events rather than textual copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality/textual independence of the narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics accused the book of being a verbatim copy of an old European work ('The Gates of Hell opened'); the publisher's offer of $100 for any such source is cited as a test of originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher invited production of any earlier work showing 'word for word' copying; absence of such a source is presented as evidence against the copying charge and thus as a criterion for judging the book's independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public accountability of press accusations (demand for evidence when condemning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author demanded that newspapers which pronounced the book 'utterly false' should publish what parts they considered false and what their evidence was, treating public justification as a standard of fair criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors were invited to specify evidence supporting their denunciations; failure or refusal to supply such evidence is described as an abdication of journalistic responsibility and is used to question the validity of their rejections.
